source_text: Sed bene quod nos onere talium personarum prior levasti. Nam in libro quem ad Timasium contra liberum arbitrium texuisti, cum sanctus Pelagius venerabilium virorum tam Ambrosii quam Cypriani recordatus fuisset, qui liberum arbitrium in libris suis commendaverant, respondisti nulla te gravari auctoritate talium; ita ut diceres, eos processu vitae melioris, si quid male senserant, expiasse [n164] . Tua tibi ad hoc relata sint, ut excitare de solis nominibus erubescas invidiam. Ceterum vel Ambrosii dicta, vel aliorum, quorum famam vestrorum nitimini maculare consortio, clara benignaque possunt ratione defendi.
pass_a_gloss: But it is well that you first lifted us from the burden of such persons. For in the book which you wove to Timasius against free decision, when holy Pelagius had recalled venerable men both Ambrose and Cyprian, who had commended free decision in their books, you replied that you were weighed by no authority of such; so that you said that they, by the progress of a better life, if they had sensed something badly, had expiated it. Let your own things be reported to you for this, that you may blush to stir spite from names alone. For the rest, either Ambrose's sayings, or those of others whose fame you strive to stain by fellowship of yours, can be defended by a clear and kind reason.

lemmas.lexica: LS arbitrium=judgment, free decision; Blaise liberum arbitrium
LS liber=free; Blaise unde liberum est abstinere
LS ratio; Blaise use of reason required for sin

pass_b_english: But fortunately you first relieved me of the burden of such persons. In the book you composed to Timasius against free choice, holy Pelagius had recalled venerable men, both Ambrose and Cyprian, who had commended free choice in their books. You replied that their authority placed no burden upon you, even saying that if they had thought anything wrongly, they had atoned for it through progress toward a better life (compare Augustine, On Nature and Grace 71). Let your own words be returned to you so that you are ashamed to stir hostility from names alone. Yet the statements of Ambrose and the others whose reputation you strive to stain by associating them with your party can be defended by clear and kindly reasoning.

choices.why: Glossary default: arbitrium is the decision-power, not a later Augustinian/Reformation free-will locus.
Freedom to abstain is required for will and sin.
For Julian, sin requires rational choice; infants lack usus rationis.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
